behavior.overview: This repository is a full-stack e-commerce application consisting of a Django-based backend API and a React frontend. It provides standard e-commerce functionality including user authentication, product catalog management, review systems, order processing, and payment handling.

partitions.name: Backend API (Django)
partitions.role: The backend provides RESTful APIs for data management and business logic.
partitions.functionality: Handles data models and API endpoints for user accounts, product inventory, customer reviews, shipping addresses, order management, and payment processing.

partitions.name: Frontend (React)
partitions.role: The frontend provides the user interface and interacts with the backend API.
partitions.functionality: Includes React screens and components for user navigation, product browsing, cart management, checkout flows, and user profile management, coordinated by Redux for state management.

partitions.name: Static Assets
partitions.functionality: Contains user-uploaded product images, frontend icons, and compiled CSS/JS files required for rendering the UI and serving administrative views.

partitions.name: Infrastructure
partitions.functionality: Defines the environment configuration, Docker container setup, and general project management for running the application.

context_record.business_goal: Modernize the existing e-commerce monolith to improve scalability, maintainability, and support incremental evolution without downtime.
context_record.problem_statement: The existing monolith suffers from performance degradation during peak traffic and maintainability challenges.

blueprint.selected_pattern: Strangler Fig migration from Django monolith to a small set of event-enabled services behind an API gateway
blueprint.rationale: The business goal is incremental modernization without downtime, so the pattern must name the transition rather than only its endpoint. The existing Django monolith (ecommerce/user, product, review, order, payment, address, core) already exposes REST endpoints consumed by a React frontend via frontend/src/apis/*.js, which gives a natural seam: a routing layer in front of the monolith can move one capability at a time to an extracted service while the React frontend stays unchanged. Decomposition is driven by scaling and consistency characteristics, not by Django app count: read-heavy browsing/search scales independently of checkout, cart is high-churn and ephemeral, order/inventory/fulfilment share one transactional boundary, payment needs security isolation around the external provider, and reviews must be able to fail without blocking purchase. This yields the smallest decomposition that satisfies the stated peak-traffic, availability and maintainability drivers while keeping the monolith in production throughout.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Customers keep using the same storefront throughout the modernization: they register and sign in, browse and search the catalog, manage a cart, check out and pay, track orders and leave reviews. Administrators keep managing catalog, customers, stock, orders, refunds and review moderation. The business value is that peak shopping periods (promotions, seasonal peaks) no longer degrade the whole platform, because the capabilities that carry peak read traffic (catalog, search, cart) can be scaled and released independently of checkout and order processing. Releases become incremental and reversible: each capability is moved behind a routing layer and can be switched back to the monolith if a defect appears, so modernization does not require a big-bang cutover or a customer-visible outage. A non-critical capability failing (for example reviews or search) degrades gracefully instead of taking down browsing and checkout. Measurable responsiveness and availability targets are agreed with the business and reported continuously; exact numeric targets are not yet stated and must be agreed before load testing.
blueprint.technical_view: The React Storefront continues to call a single HTTP origin, now the API Gateway and Strangler Router. The router holds per-capability, per-percentage routing rules that send a request either to the Legacy Django Monolith or to an extracted service, and it terminates authentication by validating tokens issued by the Identity and Account Service. Extracted services are independently deployable Django REST Framework applications, each owning its own PostgreSQL schema/database: Identity and Account Service (accounts, profiles, addresses, admin user management), Catalog and Search Service (products, variants, images, publication state, plus query-side search over the Product Search Index), Cart Service (guest and account carts in the Cart Data Store), Order Management Service (order lifecycle, stock reservation and inventory, shipment/fulfilment records), Payment Service (authorization, capture and refund against the external Payment Provider), and Review Service (review capture, moderation and rating aggregates). Synchronous calls are used only where a request needs an immediate answer (checkout asking Payment Service to authorize, Cart Service asking Catalog and Search Service for price/availability). Everything else is asynchronous over the Event Backbone: order placed/cancelled/dispatched, payment authorized/failed/refunded, product published/updated, review approved. The Notification Service and the Product Search Index projection are event consumers, which keeps catalog indexing and customer notifications off the request path. Observability and Monitoring Platform collects latency percentiles, error rates, health-check state and correlation-id traces from every runtime component so responsiveness and availability can be evidenced. All runtime components are stateless containers behind health checks, allowing rolling deployments and horizontal scaling per capability. The legacy monolith remains deployed and authoritative for any capability not yet extracted, and is retired only when no routing rule points at it.

constraints_addressed: Scalability: read-heavy Catalog and Search Service, Cart Service and the Product Search Index scale horizontally and independently of Order Management Service and Payment Service
High availability: stateless containers with health checks, rolling deployments, and graceful degradation of Review Service and search
No-downtime incremental evolution: per-capability routing in the API Gateway and Strangler Router with reversible cutovers, frontend unchanged
Migration: Legacy Django Monolith stays authoritative until each capability is cut over; ownership of data moves one capability at a time
Budget: no budget was stated; the design deliberately keeps the smallest viable service count and reuses the existing Django and React stack to limit rebuild and operational cost
Cloud: no provider was stated; the design is container-based and cloud-agnostic, deployable on any managed container platform
Compliance: no formal regime was stated, but card data is never stored â€” the Payment Service delegates card handling to the external Payment Provider
assumptions: ASSUMPTION: The monolith's current relational database is PostgreSQL or an equivalent RDBMS that can be split per service; the repository shows Django ORM migrations but not the engine.
ASSUMPTION: The external Payment Provider is PayPal or an equivalent hosted provider, inferred from the frontend dependencies @paypal/paypal-js and react-paypal-button-v2.
ASSUMPTION: A container orchestration platform is available or can be procured; the repository contains only a local Docker Compose setup (compose/django/local/Dockerfile).

ASSUMPTION: Numeric latency, error-rate, availability and peak-multiple targets are not yet defined; they must be agreed with stakeholders before load testing and are referenced here only qualitatively.
ASSUMPTION: The React Storefront can be pointed at a single gateway origin without functional change, since API access is already centralized in frontend/src/apis/*.js.
ASSUMPTION: Notification channels (email/SMS provider) will be selected during implementation; none exists in the repository.
open_risks: Data ownership split for order-related reads: the monolith's ecommerce/order/serializers.py joins user, address, product and payment data, so extracted services must replace these joins with API calls or read projections â€” a source of latency and consistency risk.
Eventual consistency becomes customer-visible (search index freshness, availability display, review aggregates); acceptable windows must be agreed per capability.
Dual-write or change-data-capture during each cutover can drift; reconciliation checks are required before each capability is declared migrated.
The repository has near-zero automated tests (all tests.py files are 2 LOC), so the regression safety net required by FEAT-014 must be built before the first extraction.
Operational complexity and cost increase with six services plus an event backbone and search index; without a defined budget this may need to be trimmed further.
Distributed checkout across Order Management Service and Payment Service requires idempotency keys and compensations; incorrect implementation risks duplicate orders or orphaned authorizations.

migration_steps.title: Establish regression safety net, observability and the routing seam
migration_steps.objective: Create the preconditions for any reversible extraction: a way to route traffic per capability, and the ability to see whether a cutover made things worse. This is first because no extraction is safely reversible without it.
changes: Introduce the API Gateway and Strangler Router in front of the Legacy Django Monolith with all routes initially pointing at the monolith
Point the React Storefront at the gateway origin instead of the monolith directly
Deploy the Observability and Monitoring Platform and instrument the Legacy Django Monolith and API Gateway and Strangler Router with correlation ids, latency, error-rate and health endpoints
Build automated API regression tests covering the functional requirements currently served by the Legacy Django Monolith
Provision the Event Backbone and containerize the Legacy Django Monolith for the target platform
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: No data moves. The Legacy Django Monolith remains the single source of truth for all data; the gateway is a transparent pass-through whose routing rules are configuration, not code.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All storefront traffic flows through the API Gateway and Strangler Router with baseline latency, error-rate and availability dashboards published, and the regression suite passes against the monolith.

migration_steps.title: Extract Catalog and Search Service with the Product Search Index
migration_steps.objective: Move the highest-volume, read-dominant, lowest-transactional-risk capability first so peak-traffic relief is achieved early and the extraction pattern is proven on low-risk traffic.
changes: Stand up Catalog and Search Service owning product, variant and image data, extracted from the monolith's product app
Stand up the Product Search Index and populate it as an event-driven projection from Catalog and Search Service
Route catalog browsing, product detail and product search paths through the API Gateway and Strangler Router to the new service by increasing percentage
Publish ProductPublished and ProductUpdated events on the Event Backbone
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Catalog and Search Service becomes the write owner of catalog data; the Legacy Django Monolith reads catalog data through the new service's API during the overlap and its catalog tables are frozen after cutover. Reversal is a routing-rule change back to the monolith while catalog writes are still replayable.
migration_steps.exit_condition: 100% of catalog and search traffic is served by Catalog and Search Service, search results reflect catalog edits within the agreed indexing window, and monolith catalog writes are disabled.

migration_steps.title: Extract Identity and Account Service and centralize token validation
migration_steps.objective: Identity is a cross-cutting dependency of every remaining capability, so it must be extracted before the transactional capabilities that depend on it. It also carries a distinct security boundary.
changes: Stand up Identity and Account Service owning accounts, profiles, credentials and shipping/billing addresses (monolith user, core and address apps)
Issue and validate tokens centrally; configure the API Gateway and Strangler Router to validate tokens against Identity and Account Service
Route registration, login, password reset, profile, address and admin user management endpoints to the new service
Publish AccountCreated and AccountDeactivated events on the Event Backbone
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Accounts and addresses are migrated with a one-time backfill followed by change-data capture from the monolith until write traffic is fully cut over; the Legacy Django Monolith continues to accept the new tokens so partially migrated flows keep working. Reversal reverts routing while the monolith tables remain synchronized.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All authentication and account traffic is served by Identity and Account Service, tokens are honoured by both the monolith and extracted services, and the account backfill reconciles with zero unexplained differences.

migration_steps.title: Extract Cart Service with the Cart Data Store
migration_steps.objective: Cart is high-churn, short-lived state whose scaling profile matches browsing rather than order processing; moving it before checkout removes cart write load from the monolith database and prepares the checkout extraction.
changes: Stand up Cart Service backed by the Cart Data Store for guest and account carts, including guest-to-account cart merge on login
Cart Service calls Catalog and Search Service for current price and availability
Route cart endpoints through the API Gateway and Strangler Router to Cart Service
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Carts are transient, so no historical backfill is required: new carts are created in the Cart Data Store while carts already open in the Legacy Django Monolith are drained until expiry. The monolith checkout reads the cart through Cart Service during the overlap.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All cart operations are served by Cart Service, guest carts merge correctly on login, and no new carts are created in the monolith.

migration_steps.title: Extract Payment Service around the external Payment Provider
migration_steps.objective: Isolate provider integration and payment records behind a narrow interface before order and checkout logic moves, so the transactional extraction that follows only has to integrate with one stable payment API.
changes: Stand up Payment Service owning payment records, authorization/capture/refund flows and Payment Provider webhooks
Publish PaymentAuthorized, PaymentFailed and PaymentRefunded events on the Event Backbone
Legacy Django Monolith checkout calls Payment Service instead of the provider directly
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Historical payment records are backfilled read-only into Payment Service; the Legacy Django Monolith stops writing payment rows once it calls Payment Service. Reversal restores the monolith's direct provider call path.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All authorizations, captures and refunds flow through Payment Service, provider webhooks are processed idempotently, and no card data is persisted anywhere in the platform.

migration_steps.title: Extract Order Management Service covering orders, inventory and fulfilment
migration_steps.objective: Move the transactional core last, as a single consistency boundary, because order lifecycle, stock reservation and shipment records must not be split across services without distributed transactions. All of its dependencies are already extracted at this point.
changes: Stand up Order Management Service owning order lifecycle, per-variant stock and reservations, and shipment/fulfilment records
Implement idempotent checkout submission coordinating Cart Service, Payment Service and stock reservation
Route checkout, order history, order detail, cancellation and admin order/stock endpoints to Order Management Service

adrs.title: ADR-001: Modernize via a Strangler Fig migration behind an API gateway rather than a big-bang rewrite
adrs.context: The business requires improved scalability and maintainability with incremental evolution and no downtime. The existing system is a Django monolith with a React frontend whose API calls are already centralized in frontend/src/apis/*.js, and the repository contains effectively no automated tests (every tests.py is 2 LOC).
adrs.decision: Introduce an API Gateway and Strangler Router in front of the Legacy Django Monolith and migrate capabilities one at a time, with per-capability, percentage-based routing and reversible cutovers, until the monolith carries no traffic and is retired.
adrs.rationale: A big-bang rewrite cannot satisfy 'without downtime' and is unacceptably risky with no regression suite. Routing at a single origin lets the React Storefront stay unchanged while each capability moves, and lets a defective cutover be reverted by configuration. It also allows scaling relief to be delivered early (catalog and search) instead of at the end of a multi-quarter rewrite.
alternatives_considered: Big-bang rewrite to microservices
Keep the monolith and scale it vertically / add caching only
Frontend-side routing between old and new APIs
positive_consequences: Every cutover is reversible by a routing rule change
The React Storefront requires no change per migration step
Scaling benefit is realized incrementally
negative_consequences: Two systems must be operated and kept consistent during the transition
The gateway becomes a critical path component requiring its own redundancy

adrs.title: ADR-002: Retain Python/Django REST Framework and React as the default implementation stack for extracted services
adrs.context: The detected stack is Python/Django on the backend (ecommerce/*/views.py, serializers.py, Django migrations) and React with Redux on the frontend. No requirement names a different language or framework.
adrs.decision: Implement every extracted service as a Django REST Framework application in Python, reusing the existing models, serializers and view logic where possible, and keep the React Storefront as the customer-facing UI. Only two specialized stores deviate: the Product Search Index and the Cart Data Store (see ADR-005 and ADR-006).
adrs.rationale: The existing code is the fastest and lowest-risk path to a working extracted service: models, serializers and admin already encode the domain rules. No stated requirement â€” peak traffic, availability, responsiveness â€” is unreachable with horizontally scaled Django processes behind a gateway. Changing language or framework would discard working domain logic and add rewrite risk with no requirement-linked benefit.
alternatives_considered: Rewrite services in Go or Node.js for microservice fashion
Replace React with a server-rendered framework
positive_consequences: Domain logic and migrations are reused rather than reimplemented
Existing team skills apply unchanged
Lower cost, relevant given no stated budget
negative_consequences: Python process-per-request concurrency requires more instances than an async runtime for the same throughput
Shared behaviour in ecommerce/core/behaviours.py must be duplicated or packaged as a shared library, risking coupling

adrs.title: ADR-003: Decompose by scaling and transactional boundaries into six services, not one service per Django app
adrs.context: The monolith has seven Django apps (user, core, address, product, review, order, payment). A naive mapping would produce seven services, splitting the order/payment/inventory transaction across process boundaries and creating services with no independent scaling or ownership driver.
adrs.decision: Extract six services: Identity and Account Service (user, core, address â€” one identity/security boundary), Catalog and Search Service (product plus search â€” read-heavy, independently scaled), Cart Service (high-churn ephemeral state), Order Management Service (orders, inventory and fulfilment â€” one transactional consistency boundary), Payment Service (security isolation around the external provider), and Review Service (non-critical, must degrade independently). Address data stays with Identity and Account Service rather than becoming its own service.
adrs.rationale: Each boundary is justified by a concrete driver. Catalog and search carry the peak read traffic and must scale separately from checkout (FEAT-011). Cart writes are frequent, short-lived and session-scoped, a different data-access pattern from durable order data. Orders, stock reservation and fulfilment mutate together at checkout and cancellation; splitting them would require distributed transactions to keep stock non-negative (FEAT-008). Payment isolates the provider integration and avoids card data spreading. Reviews are 'should' priority and must fail without blocking purchase (FEAT-012). The address and core (country/state/city) apps are tiny and only referenced by user and order serializers â€” they get no separate service.
alternatives_considered: One microservice per Django app (seven services)
A single modular monolith with no extraction
Two services only: read side and write side
positive_consequences: Read-heavy and transactional traffic scale independently
Checkout stays within a single transactional boundary
Operational surface is kept as small as the requirements allow
negative_consequences: Order Management Service is comparatively large and may need further splitting if fulfilment volume grows
Cross-service reads that were SQL joins in ecommerce/order/serializers.py become API calls or projections

adrs.title: ADR-004: Adopt an event backbone for asynchronous integration between services
adrs.context: Order, payment, stock, notification and review-aggregate updates cross service boundaries. Doing all of this synchronously would couple availability: a slow Notification Service or search reindex would slow or fail checkout.
adrs.decision: Introduce an Event Backbone carrying domain events (OrderPlaced, OrderCancelled, OrderDispatched, OrderDelivered, StockChanged, PaymentAuthorized, PaymentFailed, PaymentRefunded, ProductPublished, ProductUpdated, ReviewApproved, AccountCreated). Synchronous calls are reserved for interactions that need an immediate answer, principally checkout to Payment Service and cart pricing to Catalog and Search Service.
adrs.rationale: E-commerce business processes are inherently event-oriented, and asynchronous propagation decouples availability and lets non-critical consumers (Notification Service, Product Search Index projection) fail or lag without blocking the revenue path â€” directly serving the graceful-degradation criterion in FEAT-012.
alternatives_considered: Purely synchronous REST between services
Database-level replication between services
Scheduled batch synchronization
positive_consequences: Non-critical capabilities cannot block checkout
New consumers can be added without changing producers
The monolith can consume and produce events during coexistence
negative_consequences: Eventual consistency becomes visible (search freshness, availability display, rating aggregates)
Requires idempotent consumers, retry and dead-letter handling
Adds a critical piece of infrastructure to operate

adrs.title: ADR-005: Serve product search from a dedicated search index maintained as an event-driven projection
adrs.context: FEAT-004 requires relevance ranking, typo tolerance, combinable filters and accurate facet counts. The monolith serves listings from Django ORM queries in ecommerce/product/views.py against the relational store, which cannot provide fuzzy matching or facet counts efficiently at peak read load.
adrs.decision: Introduce a Product Search Index (search engine such as OpenSearch/Elasticsearch) owned by Catalog and Search Service, populated as a projection from catalog events, and serve keyword search and faceted filtering from it while the relational catalog store remains the system of record.
adrs.rationale: This is a data-access pattern the current store cannot meet cleanly, which is the justification required to add a technology beyond the detected stack. Keeping the relational store authoritative preserves the existing Django models and migrations; only the query path changes.
alternatives_considered: PostgreSQL full-text search with trigram similarity
Keeping ORM LIKE queries and adding caching
A third-party hosted search SaaS
positive_consequences: Typo-tolerant, ranked, faceted search becomes feasible
Search read load is isolated from the transactional catalog store
negative_consequences: Index freshness lag must be agreed and monitored
An additional stateful system to operate and secure
Reindexing procedures must be built and tested

adrs.title: ADR-006: Hold cart state in a dedicated low-latency key-value store owned by Cart Service
adrs.context: The current implementation keeps cart state in the React Redux store (frontend/src/store/cart) with no server-side cart, so guest carts do not survive device changes and cannot be merged reliably. FEAT-005 requires server-side persistence, session-scoped guest carts and merge on login at peak load.
adrs.decision: Cart Service owns cart state in a Cart Data Store (in-memory key-value store with persistence, e.g. Redis), keyed by session id or account id, with TTL-based expiry for guest carts.
adrs.rationale: Cart writes are frequent, short-lived and never queried analytically; a key-value store with TTL matches this access pattern and avoids loading the transactional database with churn during peak browsing. This is a new capability rather than a replacement of an existing backend store, since the repository has no server-side cart persistence at all.
alternatives_considered: Relational cart tables in the order database
Keeping the cart client-side only
Cookie-based cart storage
positive_consequences: Cart survives reloads and merges deterministically on login
Peak cart churn does not touch the order database
negative_consequences: Cart durability depends on the store's persistence configuration
Another stateful component to size and monitor

adrs.title: ADR-007: Isolate payment provider integration in a Payment Service that stores no card data
adrs.context: The monolith holds payment records in ecommerce/payment and the frontend integrates a hosted provider directly (@paypal/paypal-js, react-paypal-button-v2). FEAT-006 requires that no raw card data is stored and that checkout is idempotent under duplicate submission.
adrs.decision: All provider interaction, webhook handling and payment record keeping is confined to Payment Service. Card data is captured by the provider's hosted flow and never traverses or persists in platform components; Payment Service stores only provider references, status and amounts, and exposes idempotent authorize/capture/refund operations keyed by a checkout idempotency key.
adrs.rationale: Confining the provider integration to one service is a security-isolation boundary: it minimizes the components in scope for payment-related review and keeps a single, testable place for idempotency and reconciliation logic. No formal compliance regime was stated, so the design avoids card data entirely rather than assuming a certification scope.
alternatives_considered: Keep payment logic inside Order Management Service
Continue calling the provider directly from the React Storefront
positive_consequences: Narrow security scope around payments
Single owner of provider webhooks and idempotency
Provider can be replaced behind a stable internal interface
negative_consequences: Checkout spans two services, requiring compensation on partial failure
Payment Service is on the critical revenue path and needs its own redundancy

adrs.title: ADR-008: Give each extracted service exclusive ownership of its data, migrated by backfill plus change-data capture
adrs.context: All data currently lives in one relational schema, and serializers join across apps (ecommerce/order/serializers.py imports address, payment, product and user serializers). Independent deployment and scaling are impossible while services share tables, but the migration must not lose data or require downtime.
adrs.decision: Each extracted service owns a private database or schema that no other service reads directly. Data is moved per capability with a one-time backfill followed by change-data capture from the monolith until the capability's write traffic is cut over, after which the monolith tables are frozen. Cross-service reads are replaced by API calls or event-fed read projections.
adrs.rationale: Exclusive data ownership is what makes independent deployment and per-capability scaling real; without it the services are a distributed monolith. Backfill plus change-data capture keeps the old and new stores consistent during the reversible window required by FEAT-014, avoiding a downtime cutover.
alternatives_considered: Shared database across all services
Dual writes from application code
Offline cutover during a maintenance window
positive_consequences: Services deploy and scale independently
Cutovers stay reversible while capture is running
Blast radius of a schema change is one service
negative_consequences: Cross-service joins become API calls or projections, adding latency
Capture pipelines can drift and need reconciliation checks
Referential integrity across boundaries becomes an application concern

adrs.title: ADR-009: Run all runtime components as stateless containers with health checks, rolling deployment and centralized observability
adrs.context: FEAT-011, FEAT-012 and FEAT-013 require horizontal capacity increase without code change, deployments with no customer-visible downtime, automatic replacement of unhealthy instances, and continuous measurement of latency, error rate and availability. The repository only contains a local Docker Compose setup and no monitoring. No cloud provider or budget was specified.
adrs.decision: Deploy every service, the API Gateway and Strangler Router and the Legacy Django Monolith as stateless containers on a managed container platform, each exposing liveness/readiness endpoints, deployed with a rolling strategy and automated rollback, and emitting metrics, structured logs and correlation-id traces to the Observability and Monitoring Platform. Numeric latency, error-rate, availability and peak-multiple targets are to be agreed with stakeholders and then encoded as alert thresholds and load-test criteria.
adrs.rationale: Statelessness plus health checks is what makes 'add instances to add capacity' and 'replace an unhealthy instance' true rather than aspirational, and a cloud-agnostic container platform avoids committing to a provider that has not been chosen. Targets are left qualitative here because the Context Record states the magnitude as unknown.
alternatives_considered: Virtual machines with manual scaling
Serverless functions per capability
Committing now to one specific cloud provider's managed services
positive_consequences: Per-capability horizontal scaling and rolling releases
Responsiveness and availability can be evidenced per period
Deployment approach remains portable across providers
negative_consequences: Platform operations skills and tooling are required
Observability infrastructure carries ongoing cost, unbudgeted so far
Without agreed numeric targets, alert thresholds are provisional

scalability_considerations: Partitioned per aggregate key to preserve ordering while scaling consumers
Replicated brokers so a broker loss does not stop event flow
Consumer lag monitored as an early warning of peak overload

components.name: Observability and Monitoring Platform
components.purpose: Measures and reports latency, error rate, availability and traces so responsiveness objectives can be verified and alerted on.
components.description: Central metrics, logging, tracing and alerting stack. It records latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), throughput and error rate per customer-facing capability, exposes dashboards comparing them to the agreed targets, correlates requests end to end via a correlation identifier propagated by the API Gateway and Strangler Router, drives health-check-based instance replacement, and produces per-period reports evidencing whether responsiveness and availability targets were met. Numeric thresholds are configured once stakeholders agree them. Migration disposition: new component introduced in migration step 1, before any extraction, so cutovers can be judged against a baseline.
inputs: Metrics, structured logs, traces and health-check results from every runtime component
outputs: Dashboards, alerts and periodic responsiveness/availability reports
technology_choices: OpenTelemetry instrumentation
Prometheus-compatible metrics with Grafana dashboards
Centralized log aggregation and distributed tracing backend
security_considerations: Logs scrubbed of credentials, tokens and personal data
Dashboard and alert access restricted to authorized operators
Retention policy aligned with data-protection expectations
scalability_considerations: Sampling for traces at peak load to bound ingestion cost
Retention tiering to control storage growth, relevant given no stated budget

components.name: Payment Provider
components.purpose: External hosted payment provider that captures card details and performs authorization, capture and refund.
components.description: Third-party provider (assumed PayPal or equivalent, inferred from the frontend dependencies @paypal/paypal-js and react-paypal-button-v2) whose hosted flow captures payment credentials so the platform never handles card data. Migration disposition: external/already existing; only the integration point moves, from the Legacy Django Monolith and React Storefront to Payment Service in migration step 5.
inputs: Authorization, capture and refund calls from Payment Service
Card details entered by the Customer in the provider-hosted flow
outputs: Payment results and webhook callbacks to Payment Service
technology_choices: Existing hosted provider integration retained
security_considerations: Card data remains within the provider's scope
Webhook authenticity verified by signature
scalability_considerations: Provider rate limits and availability are outside platform control; failures must degrade to a clear, actionable checkout error

judgment_reasons.repo_grounding: The design repeatedly cites concrete repository facts: seven Django apps (user, core, address, product, review, order, payment), frontend/src/apis/*.js as the centralized API seam, ecommerce/order/serializers.py cross-app joins, the client-only Redux cart in frontend/src/store/cart, near-zero tests (all tests.py 2 LOC), @paypal/paypal-js and react-paypal-button-v2 dependencies, compose/django/local/Dockerfile as only local container setup, and ecommerce/media for product images. ADR-003 explicitly rejects a naive app-per-service mapping using observed app sizes and dependency edges.
judgment_reasons.flaw_detection: The design targets the stated goal (peak-traffic scalability, maintainability, incremental no-downtime evolution) at its structural cause: a single Django process/database where read-heavy catalog/search, high-churn cart, and transactional checkout share capacity and a schema (evidenced by shared behaviours.py and cross-app serializer joins). Decomposition is boundary-justified rather than module-mirroring â€” address and core are folded into Identity rather than becoming tiny services, and orders/inventory/fulfilment are deliberately kept together to avoid distributed transactions on stock. Migration_steps are coherent: routing seam + observability + regression tests first, catalog/search (low risk, high peak relief) next, identity before dependent capabilities, cart, payment before order so checkout integrates a stable interface, order last, reviews/notifications, then monolith retirement. Each step states coexistence/data strategy (backfill + CDC, frozen tables, TTL drain for carts, routing-by-creation-date for in-flight orders) and reversibility, with no big-bang cutover.
judgment_reasons.adr_soundness: ADRs carry real alternatives and honest negative consequences (gateway as critical path, Python concurrency cost, eventual consistency, CDC drift, two systems in flight). Technology changes from the detected stack are requirement-linked: ADR-002 explicitly retains Django/DRF and React and rejects rewriting in Go/Node as unjustified; the only new stores are the search index (ADR-005, justified by FEAT-004 typo tolerance/facets/peak read load that ORM LIKE queries cannot serve) and Redis cart store (ADR-006, justified by absence of any server-side cart plus FEAT-005 merge/persistence and write-churn isolation). Event backbone (ADR-004) is tied to the graceful-degradation criterion of FEAT-012, and per-service data ownership (ADR-008) is tied to the reversibility window of FEAT-014.
judgment_reasons.best_practice_grounding: Source references point to actual repository files (ecommerce/product/views.py, ecommerce/order/serializers.py, ecommerce/payment/models.py) and to the three supplied research documents, whose content (event-oriented e-commerce processes, per-service scaling under promotional peaks, monolith scalability/maintenance limits) matches the claims made. Uncertainty is labelled rather than asserted: six explicit ASSUMPTION entries (DB engine, PayPal inference, orchestration platform, undefined numeric targets, gateway origin repointing, notification provider) and six open risks including CDC drift, missing regression suite, and operational cost of six services.
judgment_reasons.refinement_readiness: All four preceding judgments pass; remaining items are already surfaced as explicit assumptions and open risks with named owners of the gap (e.g. numeric latency/availability targets to be agreed before load testing, reconciliation checks required before declaring a capability migrated).

Microservices architecture has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the promise of enhanced scalability, improved fault tolerance, and greater development agility [1]. By decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, independently deployable services, organizations can achieve better resource utilization, faster deployment cycles, and improved system resilience.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) patterns have gained particular attention in the context of microservices migration, especially for e-commerce systems where business processes are inherently event-oriented. Customer actions such as placing orders, updating profiles, or processing payments naturally translate to domain events that can drive system behavior [5]. The asynchronous nature of event-driven communication provides better decoupling between services, enhanced fault tolerance, and improved scalability compared to synchronous request-response patterns [4].

ModernizingÂ to microservices
Microservices are essentially small, independent units that make up an application. Transitioning 
from traditional monolithic structures to microservices can follow various strategies.
Are you Well-Architected? 2

## 2.2 Monolithic and Microservices Architectures Comparison *(printed p. 478)*

In the e-commerce landscape, choosing between microservices and traditional monolithic architectures requires careful consideration of various factors. Monolithic architectures, characterized by their single, tightly coupled codebase. However, when e-commerce systems increase in size, they frequently face scalability and maintenance issues. Microservices provide an alternative approach by decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, self-contained services [6]. This decomposition results in fine-grained services, each focusing on a specific business capability. Scalability is one of the most major advantages of microservices. E-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic patterns, especially during promotions or seasonal events. Microservices enable organisations to scale individual services, ensuring that resources are deployed efficiently to manage workload properly.

features.name: Customer Registration and Authentication
features.description: Customers can create an account with email and password, verify their email, log in, log out, and reset a forgotten password. Sessions are issued as tokens usable across customer-facing services.
features.scenario: A new visitor registers with a unique email and password, receives a verification email, activates the account, then logs in successfully and receives a valid session token; a second registration attempt with the same email is rejected.
acceptance_criteria: Registration with a unique, well-formed email and policy-compliant password creates an account in pending-verification state
Duplicate email registration returns a clear validation error and creates no account
Login with correct credentials returns an authenticated session/token; incorrect credentials are rejected without revealing which field failed
Password reset link is single-use and expires after a defined period
Login and registration requests complete within the agreed responsive latency budget under normal load

features.name: User Account and Profile Management
features.description: Authenticated users can view and update profile details, manage multiple shipping and billing addresses, change password, and view their order history entry points. Administrators can view and manage customer accounts.
features.scenario: A logged-in customer updates their display name, adds a second shipping address, sets it as default, and changes their password; the next checkout pre-selects the new default address.
acceptance_criteria: Profile changes persist and are immediately reflected on reload
A customer can store multiple addresses and designate exactly one default shipping and one default billing address
Password change requires the current password and invalidates other active sessions
Unauthenticated or cross-account access to a profile returns an authorization error
Administrators can search for and view customer accounts and deactivate an account

features.name: Product Catalog and Browsing
features.description: Customers can browse products by category, view paginated product listings, and open a product detail page showing description, images, price, variants, and availability. Administrators can create, update, publish, and unpublish catalog entries.
features.scenario: A customer opens the 'Footwear' category, pages through results, sorts by price, and opens a product detail page showing the current price, images, variants, and in-stock status.
acceptance_criteria: Category listings return paginated results with stable ordering and support sorting by price and newest
Product detail page shows description, images, price, variants and current availability
Unpublished or deleted products are not reachable from customer-facing browsing and return a not-found response
Administrator catalog changes become visible to customers within the agreed propagation window
Catalog listing and detail responses meet the responsive latency budget at target peak load

features.name: Product Search and Filtering
features.description: Customers can perform keyword search across product titles, descriptions and attributes, with filters (category, price range, availability, rating) and facet counts, tolerant of minor typos.
features.scenario: A customer types 'runing shoes', receives relevant running-shoe results despite the typo, filters to price 50-100 and in-stock only, and the result count updates accordingly.
acceptance_criteria: Keyword search returns relevance-ranked results including matches with minor spelling errors
Filters for category, price range, availability and rating can be combined and reflect accurate facet counts
Search returns an empty-state message with suggestions when there are no matches
Newly published or edited products appear in search results within the agreed indexing window
Search responses meet the responsive latency budget at target peak load

features.name: Shopping Cart
features.description: Customers can add, update quantity of, and remove items in a cart. Guest carts persist by session and merge into the account cart on login. Cart totals reflect current prices and availability.
features.scenario: A guest adds two items to the cart, logs in, and finds both items merged with the three items previously saved in their account cart, with a single correct subtotal.
acceptance_criteria: Adding, updating and removing items recalculates line totals and subtotal correctly
Guest cart contents survive page reloads within the session lifetime
On login, guest cart items merge into the account cart without duplicating identical lines (quantities combined)
Cart flags items whose price changed or which became unavailable before checkout
Cart operations meet the responsive latency budget at target peak load

features.name: Checkout and Payment Processing
features.description: Customers complete checkout by selecting shipping address and shipping method, reviewing totals including shipping and tax, and paying via a payment provider. Payment authorization, failure handling and idempotent order creation are included.
features.scenario: A customer with three cart items proceeds to checkout, chooses a saved address and standard shipping, pays successfully, and is shown an order confirmation with an order number; a duplicate submit of the same checkout does not create a second order.
acceptance_criteria: Checkout validates stock availability for every line before authorizing payment
Order total equals item subtotal plus shipping plus tax minus discounts and is shown before payment
Successful payment authorization creates exactly one order and empties the cart
Failed or declined payment leaves the cart intact, creates no confirmed order, and shows an actionable error
Repeated submission of the same checkout request is idempotent and yields a single order
No raw payment card data is stored by the system

features.name: Order Management and Tracking
features.description: Customers can view order history, order detail, current status and tracking information, and request cancellation while allowed. Administrators can list, filter, and update order status and issue refunds.
features.scenario: A customer opens 'My Orders', selects a recent order, sees status 'Shipped' with a carrier tracking number; an administrator later marks it 'Delivered' and the customer view reflects the change.
acceptance_criteria: Order history lists a customer's own orders only, paginated and newest-first
Order detail shows line items, totals, payment status, shipping address and status history with timestamps
Status transitions follow a defined allowed state machine and invalid transitions are rejected
Customers can cancel an order only before fulfilment starts; cancellation triggers refund and stock release
Administrators can filter orders by status, date range and customer, and record refunds

features.name: Inventory Management
features.description: Stock levels are tracked per product variant, reserved at checkout, decremented on fulfilment and released on cancellation or reservation expiry. Administrators can adjust stock and see low-stock alerts.
features.scenario: Two customers concurrently check out the last unit of an item; one order is confirmed and the other receives an out-of-stock error, and the stock level ends at zero with no negative value.
acceptance_criteria: Stock is tracked per variant and never becomes negative under concurrent checkouts
Checkout creates a time-bounded reservation that is released automatically if the order is not completed
Cancellations and refunds release reserved or deducted stock back to available
Administrators can perform manual stock adjustments with an auditable reason and actor
Products at or below the configured low-stock threshold appear in an administrator low-stock report

features.name: Shipping and Fulfilment
features.description: The system offers shipping options with cost and estimated delivery at checkout, generates fulfilment records and shipments, captures carrier tracking numbers, and notifies customers of dispatch and delivery.
features.scenario: An administrator marks a paid order as dispatched, enters the carrier and tracking number; the customer receives a dispatch notification and the tracking number appears on the order detail page.
acceptance_criteria: Checkout presents at least one shipping method with a calculated cost and delivery estimate for the destination address
Marking an order dispatched records carrier, tracking number and dispatch timestamp
Customers receive dispatch and delivery notifications for their orders
Partial shipments are supported: each shipment records its own line items and tracking data
Shipping status updates are reflected in the customer order tracking view

features.name: Product Reviews and Ratings
features.description: Customers can submit a star rating and written review for a product, view reviews with aggregate rating on the product page, and administrators can moderate (approve, reject, remove) reviews.
features.scenario: A customer who purchased a product submits a 4-star review; after administrator approval it appears on the product page and the product's average rating and review count update.
acceptance_criteria: An authenticated customer can submit exactly one rating (1-5) plus optional text per purchased product
Approved reviews are displayed on the product detail page with author name and date, paginated
Product average rating and review count recompute correctly when reviews are approved, edited or removed
Administrators can approve, reject or delete a review and rejected reviews are never publicly visible
Review submission and moderation actions are recorded with timestamps

features.name: Peak Traffic Scalability and Load Handling
features.description: Customer-facing capabilities scale horizontally to handle substantially higher peak traffic than the current monolith, with graceful degradation and protection against overload.
features.scenario: A load test drives traffic to the agreed peak-multiple target across browsing, search, cart and checkout; the system sustains the load with error rates and latency inside the agreed thresholds.
acceptance_criteria: A documented load test reproduces the target peak throughput and is part of the release process
At target peak load the error rate stays below the agreed threshold and latency stays within the agreed budget
Capacity can be increased by adding instances without code changes or downtime
Overload protection (rate limiting/throttling/queueing) prevents cascading failure and returns clear responses
Read-heavy browsing and search traffic can be scaled independently of checkout traffic

features.name: High Availability and Zero-Downtime Evolution
features.description: The platform remains available during peak periods and during deployments, with health checks, redundancy, failover, and incremental release of modernized capabilities without downtime.
features.scenario: A new version of the catalog capability is released during business hours; monitored availability shows no failed customer requests attributable to the deployment, and a failed instance is automatically replaced.
acceptance_criteria: Deployments are performed with a rolling or equivalent strategy producing no customer-visible downtime
An automated rollback path restores the previous version within the agreed recovery time
Every runtime component exposes health checks and unhealthy instances are automatically replaced or removed from traffic
Failure of a non-critical capability (e.g. reviews or search) degrades gracefully without blocking browsing, cart or checkout
Availability during defined peak periods is measured against the agreed target and reported

features.name: Responsiveness Monitoring and Observability
features.description: The system measures and reports latency, error rates, and availability for customer-facing interactions, with alerting on threshold breaches, so responsiveness objectives can be verified continuously.
features.scenario: Checkout p95 latency exceeds the agreed threshold for five consecutive minutes; an alert fires and a dashboard shows the affected capability and error rates.
acceptance_criteria: Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), throughput and error rate are recorded per customer-facing capability
Dashboards display current and historical values against the agreed targets
Alerts fire when latency, error-rate or availability thresholds are breached for a sustained window
Requests can be traced end to end across capabilities using a correlation identifier
Reports evidence whether responsiveness and availability targets were met per period

features.name: Incremental Migration from the Existing Monolith
features.description: Existing Django monolith capabilities are migrated incrementally behind the current React frontend, with traffic routing per capability, data consistency during transition, and reversible cutovers.
features.scenario: Product search traffic is routed from the monolith to the modernized search capability for 10% of users, validated, then ramped to 100%; a defect triggers an instant switch back to the monolith with no data loss.
acceptance_criteria: Traffic for a migrated capability can be routed to the old or new implementation without redeploying the frontend
Cutover of a capability can be reversed within the agreed time window with no loss of customer data
The React frontend continues to work unchanged during and after each capability migration
Data written during a transition period remains consistent between old and new implementations
Each migration step is validated by automated regression tests covering the affected functional requirements
